### Federal_Election_Commission_v_NRA_Political_Victory_Fund_jurisdictional_dismissal_1994-12-06.md

Source: [Record](../records/Federal_Election_Commission_v_NRA_Political_Victory_Fund_jurisdictional_dismissal_1994-12-06.md#public-projection).

## Event

Federal Election Commission v. NRA Political Victory Fund, No. 93-1151.

On writ of certiorari to the D.C. Circuit, reviewing 6 F.3d 821, judgment October 22, 1993, opinion amended October 25. Argued October 11, 1994; decided December 6, 1994. The antecedent questions are the Commission's independent certiorari authority and the effect of later Solicitor General authorization; only if jurisdiction exists would the Court decide the separation-of-powers objection to nonvoting congressional officers. The lower court reversed the district enforcement judgment on the structural ground and left statutory contribution and First Amendment defenses unresolved. The Commission filed its petition January 18, 1994; the later authorization is dated May 26. No restart or extension is established.

Render form: full — threshold dismissal with separate authority and constitutional-merits dissents.

## Participation

Participating at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer. Ginsburg does not participate; no public reason is stated. 8 qualified Justices constitute the participating Court; quorum is satisfied.

## Public Action

Writ dismissed for want of jurisdiction, 6–2; Ginsburg did not participate.

## Judgment & Remedy

| Component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Authority and timely invocation of Supreme Court review | Dismiss for want of jurisdiction, 6–2 | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens | Existing writ dismissed; D.C. Circuit judgment remains in place. |
| Nonvoting congressional membership; severability; structural ratification; FECA and First Amendment liability | Not reached by the Court | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer (threshold nonreach); Stevens (merits reserved) | Stone-Zsela would reject the structural defect and remand | No Supreme Court merits judgment, contribution liability, or renewed district-court enforcement order. |

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Judgment relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I and II | Thomas | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Breyer | Six votes for both threshold grounds and dismissal. |
| Dissent on independent litigation authority | Stevens | Stone-Zsela | Two votes against dismissal; would retain timely review. |
| Separate dissent on the structural merits | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Would reverse the structural judgment and remand remaining preserved issues; no Court merits holding. |

## Holdings

### The Commission lacks independent certiorari authority for this FECA enforcement action

**Holding and operative rule:** Section 437d(a)(6)'s authority to litigate and appeal civil enforcement actions through the Commission's general counsel does not displace 28 U.S.C. §518(a)'s allocation of Supreme Court representation in this FECA corporate-contribution action. The Attorney General's particular-case direction exception remains available, and the express certiorari powers in 26 U.S.C. §§9010(d) and 9040(d) remain confined to actions in which the Commission appears under those respective funding sections.

**Authority:** Part I of Justice Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Breyer: six of eight participating Justices directly adopt the rule. Stone-Zsela and Stevens dissent; Ginsburg does not participate.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that Congress did not authorize the Commission to petition independently in this enforcement action. Providence Journal establishes that authority to conduct litigation below does not necessarily include authority to represent the Government here. Congress may create an exception, and ordinary construction determines whether it has done so. Section 437d(a)(6) gives the Commission substantial enforcement autonomy, but its general appeal language must be read with section 518(a)'s specific allocation and the express certiorari grants in the presidential-funding statutes. Those grants apply only to actions brought within their respective sections; this corporate-contribution action is not one of them. Enforcement exclusivity and the separate power to defend actions do not settle who may affirmatively invoke this Court's review. Germain permits the grants to coexist with their distinct conditions. The Court adopts neither a rule that appeal invariably excludes certiorari nor a required formula for statutory exceptions. Lawful particular-case direction remains possible; no timely direction is established here.

**Precedent treatment:**

- United States v. Providence Journal Co., 485 U.S. 693 (1988): applies its separation of lower-court litigation authority from Supreme Court representation while retaining ordinary statutory construction of congressional exceptions; no special verbal formula is imposed.
- Connecticut National Bank v. Germain, 503 U.S. 249 (1992): applies its preservation of coexisting statutory routes and their conditions; enforcement authority and Supreme Court representation can operate together.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding concerns this affirmative FECA enforcement petition. It does not deny the Commission the express powers supplied for funding litigation, construe every agency's litigation statute, or eliminate section 518(a)'s particular-case direction exception.

### Authorization after the statutory petition period does not ratify this filing

**Holding and operative rule:** Even assuming that the Solicitor General's May 26, 1994 authorization fully adopted the Commission's January 18 petition, it cannot relate back to validate this unauthorized invocation after the period in which an authorized petition could be filed had expired. Section 2101(c) allows ninety days and permits a Justice, for good cause, to extend the application period by no more than sixty days; the asserted authorization falls outside even that maximum under either supplied judgment date.

**Authority:** Part II of Justice Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Breyer: six direct votes. Together with Part I, this ground requires dismissal for want of jurisdiction; it is not a constitutional merits disposition.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that subsequent authorization cannot cure this petition after lawful filing became impossible. The Commission filed on January 18, within ninety days of the October 22 judgment, but lacked authority to invoke review for the Government. Cook permits ratification to relate back only when the principal could perform the act both when first attempted and when adopted. By May 26 the ninety-day period and even the maximum possible sixty-day extension had elapsed. Treating the October 25 amendment as the starting point would not change that conclusion; the Court finds neither a restart nor an extension. The fullest claimed authorization therefore fails without an inquiry into finer wording of the letter. Dodge concerned adoption of a seizure in a forfeiture proceeding, not this expired review period. Smith v. Barry preserves functional compliance by a timely notice document, not missing governmental authority. Ordinary timely corrections and lawful delegation are not foreclosed by this bounded decision.

**Precedent treatment:**

- Cook v. Tullis, 85 U.S. (18 Wall.) 332 (1873): applies the requirement that a ratifying principal have capacity both at the original act and at ratification, with intervening rights preserved; relation back does not supply capacity after this statutory petition period.
- Dodge v. United States, 272 U.S. 530 (1926): distinguishes adoption of an unauthorized seizure where the forfeiture prerequisites were satisfied from authorization of appellate review after the statutory filing period.
- Smith v. Barry, 502 U.S. 244 (1992): distinguishes a timely document that functionally supplies required appellate notice from a filing lacking governmental representation authority; the functional-notice holding remains intact.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court decides no universal rule that all representation defects are incurable. It makes no finding that a Justice granted an extension or that the amended lower opinion restarted time. The Solicitor General's authorization is distinct from any Commission resolution addressing its composition; neither constitutional validity nor structural ratification is reached.

## Precedent Treatment

- United States v. Providence Journal Co., 485 U.S. 693 (1988): applies its separation of lower-court litigation authority from Supreme Court representation while retaining ordinary statutory construction of congressional exceptions; no special verbal formula is imposed.
- Connecticut National Bank v. Germain, 503 U.S. 249 (1992): applies its preservation of coexisting statutory routes and their conditions; enforcement authority and Supreme Court representation can operate together.
- Cook v. Tullis, 85 U.S. (18 Wall.) 332 (1873): applies the requirement that a ratifying principal have capacity both at the original act and at ratification, with intervening rights preserved; relation back does not supply capacity after this statutory petition period.
- Dodge v. United States, 272 U.S. 530 (1926): distinguishes adoption of an unauthorized seizure where the forfeiture prerequisites were satisfied from authorization of appellate review after the statutory filing period.
- Smith v. Barry, 502 U.S. 244 (1992): distinguishes a timely document that functionally supplies required appellate notice from a filing lacking governmental representation authority; the functional-notice holding remains intact.

## Law After Decision

Effective December 6, 1994, the Commission's general FECA enforcement appeal power does not independently authorize this Supreme Court petition, and the assumed fullest later authorization cannot cure the filing after the lawful application period. Those threshold rules control; the D.C. Circuit's constitutional judgment remains in force for the parties without Supreme Court endorsement. The Court adds no rule about nonvoting congressional members, structural severability, agency ratification, the de facto officer doctrine, contribution liability, or constitutional relief.

## Separate Writings

Justice Stevens dissents in an opinion joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela. He reads section 437d(a)(6)'s express power to appeal a civil enforcement action through the Commission's general counsel as carrying that action through discretionary Supreme Court review. Section 518(a) itself uses appeal language broadly; the word therefore cannot decide the case without its statutory context. The Commission's exclusive enforcement role and the enacted grant to its own counsel support an exception under the ordinary-construction approach recognized in Providence Journal. The more explicit funding provisions do not negate that affirmative grant. He would retain the timely proceeding for consideration of the merits. He does not adopt later ratification as an additional ground and expresses no conclusion on the constitutionality of the nonvoting members or the underlying contribution dispute.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela also files a separate dissent on the merits. Having accepted independent litigation authority, he would reverse the separation-of-powers ground and remand for the preserved statutory and enforcement issues the Court of Appeals did not decide. He distinguishes legally operative executive control from advice, observation, communication, or persuasion. Congressional officers cannot receive a vote, veto, quorum power, binding directive, or other legal authority over execution by being called nonvoting or ex officio. On the arrangement presented, the appointed Commissioners alone exercise the enforcement powers; the nonvoting officers have no identified authority to authorize, block, suspend, or direct Commission action. The operating account reported below also excludes chairmanship, meeting calls or adjournment, and quorum participation; those operating descriptions are not additional words of the statute.

Buckley concerns officers exercising significant governmental authority; Bowsher concerns executive authority lodged in an officer controlled by Congress; and the Airports Authority decision concerns a legally effective veto over operational decisions. In his view, potential influence without comparable legal power does not establish the constitutional defect those decisions forbid. An advisory label concealing approval, disapproval, delay, compulsory direction, decisive participation, or another legal consequence would present a different case. Because he finds no defect here, he would undertake no severability or structural-ratification inquiry. His proposed remand would not automatically revive the district court's enforcement judgment while other appellate issues remain. No other Justice joins these merits views, and they establish no rule of the Court.

## Procedure After Action

The existing writ is dismissed for want of jurisdiction. The lower judgment ending this enforcement action remains undisturbed; the district court's penalty and injunction are not reinstated. There is no Supreme Court merits remand or new adjudication of the unresolved enforcement defenses. This review proceeding is terminal; no additional Court act or filing condition is ordered.

## Source Notes

[D.C. Circuit, 6 F.3d 821](https://static.case.law/f3d/6/html/0821-01.html) supports the transaction, lower judgment and reported operating arrangement. Official historical [§437d](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title2/html/USCODE-1994-title2-chap14-subchapI-sec437d.htm), [§518](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-1994-title28-section518&num=0&edition=1994), and [§2101](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-1994-title28-section2101&num=0&edition=1994) provide the controlling text. The petition and authorization dates are established; the ruling assumes the full authorization claimed without quoting an unrecovered letter. The October 25 amendment is disclosed without treating it as a new judgment. [Buckley](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/424/1), [Bowsher](https://static.case.law/us/478/html/0714-01.html), and [Airports Authority](https://static.case.law/us/501/html/0252-01.html) support only the precedent descriptions in the separate merits dissent. No decisional quotation is supplied.

### Director_Office_of_Workers_Compensation_Programs_v_Newport_News_Shipbuilding_and_Dry_Dock_Co_merits_1995-03-21.md

Source: [Record](../records/Director_Office_of_Workers_Compensation_Programs_v_Newport_News_Shipbuilding_and_Dry_Dock_Co_merits_1995-03-21.md#public-projection).

## Event

Director, Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs v. Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co., No. 93-1783. Argued January 9, 1995; decided March 21, 1995. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, reviewing its October 29, 1993 judgment, 8 F.3d 175. The question is whether the Director may independently obtain review under 33 U.S.C. §921(c) on the general administrative interest asserted in Harcum's benefits award.

Render form: compact. The judgment is unanimous, and neither the statutory result, its necessary controlling proposition and coalition, nor the component-specific remedy materially changes; the separate concurrence remains judgment-only.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer participated at argument and decision. Nine qualified Justices participated; the six-Justice quorum is satisfied and five votes are required for a judgment. No nonparticipation is established.

## Public Action

The Court affirms the Fourth Circuit insofar as it refused to entertain the Director's independent challenge to Harcum's benefits award.

## Judgment & Remedy

| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Remedy or remand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Director-initiated employee-award review under §921(c) | Affirm refusal to entertain this component, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer | No opposing vote | No benefits-merits review through this petition. |
| Special Fund determination under §908(f) | Outside review; no new merits judgment | The limited mandate binds the full Court | No vote on Fund merits | Leave the Fourth Circuit's separate reversal and remand intact. |

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Opinion of the Court | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer | Affirmance | Entire bounded statutory opinion; eight rationale votes. |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Ginsburg | No other Justice | Same affirmance | Case-specific statutory result; no join in the Court's complete explanation. |

## Holdings

### The Director's general administrative interest does not confer independent review

**Holding and operative rule:** The Director's general interest in correct administration of the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act does not by itself make the Director adversely affected or aggrieved under 33 U.S.C. §921(c) by this employee's unappealed benefits award. The refusal to entertain that challenge is affirmed; no rule of categorical governmental incapacity is adopted, and the separate Special Fund disposition remains undisturbed.

**Authority:** Justice O'Connor's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer: eight direct rationale votes. Justice Ginsburg concurs in the judgment and agrees with the case-specific statutory result, but does not join this explanation. No fractured-opinion synthesis is needed.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that administrative responsibility does not itself satisfy the condition Congress placed on judicial review. Section 921(c) requires a person adversely affected or aggrieved; §921(b)(3)'s administrative party-in-interest route and §939's claimant-assistance duties do not transfer Harcum's appellate entitlement to the Director. Germain requires respect for the particular statutory review route, and Gardner requires fidelity to enacted conditions rather than an administrator's preferred policy. The Director identifies no impairment of a specific entrusted function here. Harcum did not appeal, and disagreement with his award does not establish an independent adverse interest. Possible employer insolvency presents speculative Fund exposure that the requested benefits change would not reduce. Perini's treatment of respondent participation does not decide who may initiate review. Greenwich Collieries governs persuasion in covered adjudications, not this appellate entitlement. Uniform administration is important, but accepting that interest alone would erase the statutory condition. The Court reserves express governmental review authority, genuine financial or independently statutory injury, and the Director's respondent role; it decides neither compensation nor Fund liability.

**Precedent treatment:**

- Connecticut National Bank v. Germain, 503 U.S. 249: applies respect for the requirements of the particular statutory route; its bankruptcy appellate holding remains unchanged.
- Brown v. Gardner, December 12, 1994: applies fidelity to enacted conditions rather than administrative additions; its benefits-causation holding is not expanded.
- Director, OWCP v. Perini North River Associates, 459 U.S. 297: distinguishes respondent participation from a Director-initiated appeal; the respondent issue remains reserved.
- Director, OWCP v. Greenwich Collieries, June 20, 1994: preserves its persuasion-burden rules and treats them as distinct from statutory appellate entitlement.
- Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, June 12, 1992: leaves its Article III holdings unchanged; the statutory disposition makes a new constitutional rule unnecessary.

## Precedent Treatment

The Court applies Germain's respect for statutory review conditions and Gardner's fidelity to enacted limits. Perini does not resolve a right to initiate appellate review. Greenwich Collieries remains the rule for persuasion in covered adjudication, and Lujan's Article III holdings remain unchanged. No precedent is overruled, and no general restriction on Congress's capacity to authorize governmental litigation is announced.

## Law After Decision

Effective March 21, 1995, a general interest in correct administration does not alone satisfy the Director's §921(c) aggrievement requirement for this claimant's unappealed award. This adds the bounded statutory application; it does not decide all governmental aggrievement, respondent status, disability merits, or Fund liability. Congress's ability to confer an express review right and claims based on genuine financial or independently statutory injury remain open.

## Separate Writings

Justice Ginsburg concurs in the judgment. She agrees that the existing review provision does not authorize this independent challenge on the general administrative interest asserted. She does not infer that Congress deliberately intended every disparity produced by that provision. Congress may supply governmental review authority; statutory agreement here does not require endorsement of a broader account of legislative purpose. She does not decide Harcum's benefits, the Special Fund merits, or the Director's respondent role.

## Procedure After Action

The reviewed employee-award challenge ends without review of compensation merits. Harcum's unappealed award is undisturbed by this decision, as is the Fourth Circuit's separate Special Fund reversal and remand. No mandate revises §908(f) liability or awards new compensation.

## Source Notes

The [Fourth Circuit opinion, 8 F.3d 175](https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/008/8.F3d.175.92-1864.html) supplies the facts, Board proceedings, component division, and lower reasoning. The official [§921 text](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title33/html/USCODE-1994-title33-chap18-sec921.htm) and [§939 text](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title33/html/USCODE-1994-title33-chap18-sec939.htm) supply the distinct review and assistance provisions. The Court does not determine additional medical, earnings, or compensation facts.

### Swint_v_Chambers_County_Commission_merits_1995-03-01.md

Source: [Record](../records/Swint_v_Chambers_County_Commission_merits_1995-03-01.md#public-projection).

## Event

Swint v. Chambers County Commission, No. 93-1636; 514 U.S. 35. Argued January 10, 1995. Decided March 1, 1995. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, reviewing its county disposition in 5 F.3d 1435 and 11 F.3d 1030. The question is whether the county's denial of summary judgment could be reviewed during the officers' interlocutory qualified-immunity appeals.

Render form: full. The jurisdictional judgment is unanimous, but the Chief's partial joins and affirmative separate position on necessary connected review require the full opinion topology and controlling boundaries.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer participated at argument and decision. No nonparticipation is recorded.

## Public Action

The Court unanimously vacates the Commission portion of the appellate judgment and remands for dismissal of its interlocutory appeal.

## Judgment & Remedy

| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Commission's §1983 and §1985(3) appellate disposition | Vacated, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | None | Remand with instructions to dismiss the Commission's interlocutory appeal for want of appellate jurisdiction. |

The Court does not hold the Commission liable or entitled to summary judgment. The county's surviving federal claims return to their preappeal District Court posture. The officers' separate immunity dispositions remain undisturbed; the decision does not revive the separately declined City or individual state-law appeals. No county state-law count remained for decision.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relation to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I and II | Ginsburg | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer | Nine joins: adequate final review; statutory routes; no convenience-based county appeal; separability; county-only vacatur and remand. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III | Ginsburg | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer | Eight joins: independent lack of conclusiveness from the express trial-court reservation. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part IV | Ginsburg | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer | Eight joins: genuine-necessity review remains an unanswered question, not an affirmative grant or categorical prohibition. |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | None | Joins Parts I and II and the complete mandate; would recognize genuinely inseparable or necessary connected review under its stated conditions; adds no conclusiveness ground. |

## Holdings

### Ordinary municipal liability remains reviewable after final judgment

**Holding and operative rule:** The denial of this municipal defendant's ordinary liability defense does not qualify for immediate collateral-order review under §1291 because the defense remains effectively reviewable after final judgment. The officers' distinct immunity from suit does not give the municipality a corresponding right to avoid trial.

**Authority:** Part I of Justice Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer; nine Justices adopt this independently sufficient failure of collateral-order jurisdiction.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that the county must ordinarily await final judgment to obtain review of its liability defense. Cohen requires an immediately reviewable collateral order to be effectively unreviewable after final judgment, as well as conclusive and separate from the merits. Digital Equipment supplies the controlling distinction between a defense that can be vindicated on final appeal and an entitlement whose protection would be lost by undergoing trial. Mitchell recognizes immediate review of the appropriate legal qualified-immunity question because that official immunity protects against suit itself. The county has no corresponding immunity here. Its contention that Alabama law does not make the sheriff its final policymaker concerns responsibility for the alleged conduct, and that contention remains available on final review. Avoiding unnecessary litigation would be useful, but the same argument accompanies ordinary denials of summary judgment. It cannot supply the missing appellate authority. The Court expresses no view on who actually possessed county policymaking power.

**Precedent treatment:** Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. retains its cumulative collateral-order requirements. Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc. is applied through its independently controlling adequate-final-review ground. Mitchell v. Forsyth is distinguished because the officials' immunity from suit is not the county's liability defense. Monell v. Department of Social Services supplies no municipal immunity from all trial.

### The expressly tentative ruling also lacks conclusiveness

**Holding and operative rule:** An order that expressly leaves the county's final-policymaker question open for further presentation and a later legal ruling does not conclusively determine that question under Cohen. This failure independently defeats collateral-order review; the mere denial of the pending motions does not resolve a question the court expressly reserves.

**Authority:** Part III of Justice Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer; eight Justices adopt this independent ground. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela does not join this additional ground.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that the county's attribution question remained expressly open. The District Court's June opinion stated that the sheriff might have been the county's final policymaker. Its reconsideration order then promised both sides another opportunity to address that question and a legal determination before submission to the jury. Cohen requires a conclusive determination of the disputed question, and Coopers & Lybrand preserves the distinction between such a determination and a tentative ruling. The county emphasizes that reconsideration was denied and that it had to continue litigating. But final action on those pending motions did not withdraw the express reservation of the attribution question. Identifying the issue as one of law identified who must decide it, not an answer already reached. This conclusion rests on the actual reservation, rather than the abstract power to revise interlocutory orders. It does not hold that every summary-judgment denial is inconclusive or that a later conclusive ruling would satisfy the remaining appeal requirements.

**Precedent treatment:** Cohen is applied to the express reservation of the disputed question. Coopers & Lybrand v. Livesay is applied to the requirement of a conclusive, rather than tentative, determination. Neither decision is enlarged into a rule admitting every later definitive ruling to immediate appeal.

### A proper immunity appeal does not authorize this separate county appeal

**Holding and operative rule:** A court of appeals may not decide a separate party's nonappealable liability defense merely because a related officers' immunity appeal is properly before it and resolving the defense would save litigation. The county attribution issue here is neither inextricably intertwined with nor necessary to meaningful review of the officers' qualified-immunity questions, and no other authorized appellate route is established.

**Authority:** Part II of Justice Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer; nine Justices adopt this bounded rule and its application. Part IV, joined by the eight Associate Justices, leaves the availability and scope of genuinely necessary connected review undecided; the Chief's affirmative view of that possibility is separate and noncontrolling.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that efficiency cannot enlarge the appeal before the Eleventh Circuit. The officers' qualified immunity concerns violation of clearly established federal rights; the county issue concerns Alabama's assignment of policymaking authority. Common events do not make the second question necessary to answer the first. Abney confines review accompanying a double-jeopardy appeal, and United States v. Stanley likewise respects the limits of an authorized certified appeal. Their lesson is that a proper appeal does not automatically carry otherwise unreviewable matters with it. Section 1292(b) supplies a distinct, two-level permission process for qualifying interlocutory questions. No such certification and permission exist here. Congress also authorized rules defining finality and additional interlocutory categories, but that rulemaking authority does not itself admit this county appeal. The Court therefore rejects the actual convenience rationale without deciding county liability or disturbing the officers' separate appeal dispositions. No genuinely necessary connected issue is presented on these facts.

**Precedent treatment:** Abney v. United States and United States v. Stanley are applied to limits on adding otherwise unauthorized issues to a proper immediate appeal. Cohen and Digital Equipment remain the source of the separate collateral-order inquiry. Earlier examples of connected review are not overruled or converted into a general pendent-party jurisdiction doctrine.

### Statutory conditions and reserved channels

Section 1292(b) requires the District Judge's written statement that an order involves a controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and that an immediate appeal may materially advance the litigation's ultimate termination. Application must be made within ten days; the court of appeals may then permit the appeal in its discretion. Application alone does not stay District Court proceedings unless the District Judge, the court of appeals, or a judge thereof orders a stay. No qualifying certification or permission is established here. Section 1292(e) permits additional interlocutory-appeal rules prescribed under §2072; §2072(c) permits rules defining finality under §1291. Those are rulemaking authorizations, subject to §2072's prohibition on abridging, enlarging, or modifying substantive rights, and are not an operative rule allowing this appeal. No mandamus relief is sought or granted here; that distinct route retains its own requirements.

## Precedent Treatment

The holdings identify the operative treatment of Cohen, Coopers & Lybrand, Digital Equipment, Mitchell, Monell, Abney, and Stanley. No prior decision is overruled. No substantive county-liability holding is adopted from the vacated appellate ruling.

## Law After Decision

The final-judgment rule, the two independent failures of collateral-order review, and the rejection of this convenience-based appeal control. The decision does not create a general ban on every possible examination of a connected issue, and it creates no general permission either. The Chief's proposed necessary-review exception remains noncontrolling. County liability, Alabama policymaker status, the officers' ultimate liability, and any new appellate route remain undecided. The decision applies the existing rules and specifies their effect on this county appeal; it establishes no immunity or substantive civil-rights defense.

## Separate Writings

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs in part and in the judgment. He enforces the final-judgment rule and agrees that the Commission has neither an independently appealable collateral order nor a certified statutory appeal. Its responsibility under Alabama policymaker law can be reviewed after final judgment and is analytically separate from the officers' qualified immunity. He would also recognize an appellate court's authority to decide an issue genuinely inextricably intertwined with a properly appealable order or necessary to its meaningful review. That limited authority would not permit general pendent-party jurisdiction based on convenience. He leaves mandamus and §1292(b) available only under their own requirements. His affirmative recognition of genuinely necessary review goes beyond the Court's reservation; it is not a controlling holding. No Justice joins that separate proposition.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns to the Eleventh Circuit to dismiss the Commission's interlocutory appeal. The District Court may proceed on the county's surviving federal claims; any later review must rest on an independently lawful route and its actual conditions. The county appellate merits ruling is vacated, not affirmed or substituted with a new liability judgment. The separate individual rulings are unaffected.

## Source Notes

The county appeal, separate officer dispositions, and declined City and state-law appeals are documented in [Swint v. City of Wadley, 5 F.3d 1435](https://static.case.law/f3d/5/html/1435-01.html), with the later report at 11 F.3d 1030 concerning the individual proceedings. The District Court's complete June 2 and June 26, 1992 orders appear at Appendix 45a–73a of the [petition](https://archive.org/download/micro_IA40385013_0508/micro_IA40385013_0508%2002.%20Petition%20for%20Writ%20of%20Certiorari.pdf). Pages 67a and 72a supply the expressly tentative county-policymaker treatment. The later definite denial of reconsideration does not withdraw that reservation. These are procedural findings and reserved questions; the disputed raid allegations are not converted into final factual findings. Sections 1291, 1292 and 2072 are applied as in force at this decision's date.

### McKennon_v_Nashville_Banner_Publishing_Co_merits_1995-01-23.md

Source: [Record](../records/McKennon_v_Nashville_Banner_Publishing_Co_merits_1995-01-23.md#public-projection).

## Event

McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co., No. 93-1543. Argued November 2, 1994; decided January 23, 1995. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which affirmed summary judgment for the employer, 9 F.3d 539. The question is whether wrongdoing discovered after discharge bars every remedy for an age-discriminatory discharge and, if not, how it bears on available relief. Render form: compact. Basis: unanimous judgment and a common statutory liability-and-remedy rationale.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer participated at argument and decision. The Court has nine participating members.

## Public Action

Reversed and remanded, 9–0.

## Judgment & Remedy

The Sixth Circuit’s judgment is reversed and the case remanded, 9–0. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer support both rejection of the complete bar and the stated remedial rule. No Justice opposes either component. The district court must adjudicate liability without treating unknown misconduct as a cause of the original discharge and determine relief under the employer’s actual-would-discharge showing and the statutory limits. No damages amount or final liability judgment is entered.

## Opinion Topology

O'Connor delivered the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer. Every participating Justice joins each holding, its stated limits, and the judgment. No separate opinion was filed.

## Holdings

### Later-discovered misconduct does not erase an earlier ADEA violation

**Controlling proposition:** Misconduct unknown to the employer when it discharged an employee cannot defeat liability for an age-discriminatory discharge or categorically bar every remedy. The employee must still establish an ADEA violation under the governing liability rules; an employer’s assumption of discrimination for summary judgment is not a final liability finding.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion for the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. All nine adopt this proposition and explanation; it is a direct majority holding.

**Controlling explanation:** The ADEA forbids discharge because of age and gives courts authority to grant relief that serves the statute’s purposes. Hazen Paper requires age actually to motivate the challenged decision and have a determinative influence on it; a reason the employer did not know cannot have motivated it. Mt. Healthy and Price Waterhouse address lawful and unlawful reasons operating in the actual decision, so their same-decision inquiry does not transform later discovery into an original cause. The Banner assumed discrimination only to obtain summary judgment and relied on documents discovered after McKennon’s dismissal. That discovery cannot erase an otherwise proved violation. The contrary rule would remove compensation for an unlawful period and weaken enforcement whenever later investigation uncovered a sufficient ground for termination. The employee’s misconduct nevertheless matters to remedy, which the next holding addresses. The Court does not find age discrimination, change the employee’s ultimate burden, or decide whether the violation was willful.

**Precedent treatment:** Hazen Paper’s actual-motive requirement remains controlling; Mt. Healthy and Price Waterhouse are distinguished because they concern reasons involved in the challenged decision. St. Mary’s Honor Center retains its existing proof framework and does not make rejection of an employer’s explanation an automatic liability judgment.

### Proven independently sufficient misconduct limits appropriate relief

**Controlling proposition:** To limit relief through after-acquired evidence, the employer must prove misconduct so serious that it would in fact have discharged the employee for that reason alone had it known, rather than merely showing that discharge was permissible. Once that showing is made, reinstatement and front pay are ordinarily inappropriate, and backpay’s starting measure is the period from unlawful discharge to actual discovery, subject to extraordinary equitable circumstances affecting either party’s legitimate interests.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion for the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. All nine adopt the proof requirement and bounded remedial rule.

**Controlling explanation:** Section 626(b) authorizes appropriate legal and equitable relief to effectuate the ADEA, which requires attention to both discrimination and the employment consequences of serious misconduct. An order requiring continued employment or its prospective monetary substitute ordinarily makes no sense when proved wrongdoing would have ended that employment lawfully. But the employer must establish what it actually would have done; an available pretext, minor infraction, or merely possible discharge does not establish that limit. Backpay ordinarily compensates the interval before actual discovery, when the later ground had not supplied a lawful termination basis. The court may account for extraordinary equitable circumstances affecting either party’s legitimate interests, consistently with the statutory purposes. The Banner’s affidavits and McKennon’s acknowledgment supported its motion-specific would-discharge showing, but the erroneous complete bar prevented proper adjudication of liability and relief. The Court awards no amount, imposes no reinstatement decree, and leaves statutory willfulness and other distinct remedial predicates for their proper determination.

**Precedent treatment:** Hazen Paper’s knowledge-or-recklessness standard continues to govern any claim of willfulness; this remedial ruling does not lower it. Mt. Healthy and Price Waterhouse supply no complete forfeiture rule for a reason discovered after the challenged discharge.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Genuine protected opposition or participation cannot supply a lawful discharge ground; this case announces no general ban on obtaining evidence of discrimination. No final discrimination, willfulness, compensation, liquidated-damages, fee, or reinstatement finding is made. Section 626(c)(1)’s termination of the individual right to bring an action when the EEOC commences an action to enforce that employee’s right remains distinct; no such agency action is established here. The 1991 Title VII amendments supply no new rule for this ADEA discharge.

## Precedent Treatment

- Hazen Paper Co. v. Biggins preserves actual age motivation and determinative influence as the liability inquiry and knowledge or reckless disregard as the willfulness inquiry. After-acquired evidence changes neither requirement.
- Mt. Healthy City School District Board of Education v. Doyle addresses actual mixed reasons for the challenged action; it does not make an unknown later reason a complete defense.
- Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins likewise concerns contemporaneous decisionmaking and supplies no after-acquired-evidence forfeiture rule.
- St. Mary’s Honor Center v. Hicks preserves the governing burden of persuasion and rejects automatic liability from disbelief of an employer’s explanation; this decision does not alter that allocation.

## Law After Decision

Effective January 23, 1995, later-discovered misconduct supplies a possible limitation on ADEA remedies, not erasure of an otherwise proved discriminatory discharge. The employer’s actual-would-discharge burden, ordinary limits on reinstatement and front pay, and discovery-based backpay measure with extraordinary-equity consideration govern the remand. Actual age motivation, the employee’s ultimate persuasion obligation, and the separate willfulness rule remain intact.

## Separate Writings

No separate opinion was filed.

## Procedure After Action

The Sixth Circuit must return the case for proceedings consistent with the liability/remedy distinction. Liability remains to be adjudicated; any relief must rest on its statutory and factual predicates. This Court enters no amount, no final willfulness finding, and no order of reinstatement or front pay.

## Source Notes

The record and lower-court grounds appear in [9 F.3d 539](https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/009/9.F3d.539.92-5917.html), reviewing 797 F. Supp. 604. The remedial authority and its qualifications appear in [29 U.S.C. §626, 1994 edition](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-1994-title29-section626&num=0&edition=1994). The motion-specific assumption of age discrimination is not a trial finding; the opinion decides the legal effect of later-discovered misconduct and leaves unresolved liability and relief to the lower courts.
